title: Nagarjuna
hookLine: the second-century Indian philosopher of the middle way and emptiness

cards: A seed goes into the ground, and a sprout comes up. Is the sprout the same thing as the seed? Not really: the seed is gone.
Something completely different, then? Not that either: no seed, no sprout. Same doesn't fit.
Different doesn't fit. A thinker from India named Nagarjuna built a whole way of seeing on puzzles like that one.
A new part of the path begins today, the great teachers, whose thinking shaped the schools we've followed along the roads. We begin with him.

teach.b: Very little about his life is known for sure.
Tradition places him in India, centuries after the Buddha, and tells stories about him; one legend says he brought wisdom sutras up from the serpent beings, the nagas, under the sea.

Tibetan and East Asian traditions remember him as a founder of the Madhyamaka, the school of the middle. His great work, as tradition counts it, is the Mulamadhyamakakarika, the root verses on the middle way.
It starts from the Buddha's teaching that things arise from causes and conditions, and presses on it. If a thing arises only because of other things, it has no being of its own, standing apart.
His word for that is shunyata, emptiness.
It doesn't mean nothing exists. The sprout is real enough to water. It means nothing exists on its own.

In one verse, paraphrased, he says: whatever arises dependently, that is what we call emptiness; it is a name given in dependence, and it is the middle way. Not the extreme that things exist solidly, on their own.
Not the extreme that nothing exists at all. The middle. And he warns about his own idea.

Elsewhere, again in paraphrase, he says the Buddhas taught emptiness to let go of all views, and those who turn emptiness itself into a view are hard to help. The medicine isn't meant to become another thing to cling to.

how: Nagarjuna's root verses are studied and debated in Tibetan monasteries and read in East Asian schools, and Mahayana Buddhists honor him as a founder of the Madhyamaka, the middle way school.

games.q: a seed becomes a sprout. you're asked: is the sprout the same as the seed, or different?
o: neither: it arose depending on the seed.
games.why: Nagarjuna's middle way refuses both extremes: things arise dependently, neither the same nor wholly different.

practice: Pick one everyday opinion you carry, about a person, a plan, how today will go, and notice what it leans on: what you heard, what happened last time, how you slept. It's real, and it depends on other things.
Loosen your grip on it, the way you'd hold a bird, not a stone, then let it rest, and sit.

wordCard.voice: Nagarjuna. The teacher from India of the middle way, who said things are empty of being on their own, and warned against clinging even to emptiness.

orig.note: Sanskrit shunyata: emptiness, things being empty of existence on their own, Nagarjuna's central word.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle way of emptiness. Not solid, not nothing: the middle. Day nine hundred fifty-six.
